# netfox-website

The Next.js site for Netfox at https://netfox.app: landing page, docs, release notes and downloads. What the four app sites share is in the workspace's `../.claude/rules/websites.md`.

`public/appcast.xml` is the live, EdDSA-signed Sparkle feed the app polls; Netfox's `release.sh` prepends each release to it.

## Architecture

**Mantine's CSS is only what the site renders**: `theme/mantine.css` holds the rules of `@mantine/core/styles.css` for the components the code reaches, generated by `node scripts/mantine-css.mjs --write` (the same script on all four app sites). Never swap it for the per-component `styles/<C>.css`: they carry px where `styles.css` scales with the root font size. A new Mantine component fails `yarn test` until the file is regenerated.

### Theme

- The site is at night with no switch: Mantine is forced LIGHT and the night is written over it in variables (`theme/global.css`). The comments there say why. Tokens go on `:root`, never on `body`. A piece of the docs engine that reads the scheme itself (its code blocks pick Shiki's light or dark colours from `data-mantine-color-scheme`) is sent to its dark variant there too.
- A Mantine component can declare light-scheme values on its own element (Table hover, Kbd caps): override them by class, and measure contrast against the ground the text actually sits on.

### The docs engine

Since 2026-11-28 the docs run on the engine of `next-app-mantine-docs-template` (`Mantine Extensions/` workspace), not Nextra: `@next/mdx` with the content in `content/` and Nextra's `_meta` format, every piece of the interface a Mantine component. The template's `CLAUDE.md` says how it works. Removing Nextra removed `zod` (its only path) and `nextra-theme-docs`.

- **Copied from the template, byte for byte** (check with `diff -r` against it): `lib/docs/`, `lib/mdx/`, `components/shell/` (all but `DocsFooter`), `components/docs/`, `components/ColorSchemeControl/`, `components/Link/`, `app/docs/[[...slug]]/page.tsx`, `app/not-found.tsx`, `app/api/search/route.server.ts`, and the MDX block of `next.config.mjs`. A fix there goes to the template first, then here and to findergit-website in the same work; never edit them for this site alone.
- **The site's own**: `mdx-components.tsx` (the engine's elements, plus `Kbd`, `Callout`, `ShortcutsTable`, `MascotNote`, `Tutorial` without an import, and `img` = `DocsImage`), the rest of `next.config.mjs`, `components/MantineNavBar/` (the template's header with Netfox's controls), `MantineFooter` under every page, docs included (`role="contentinfo"`: the shell draws it inside `AppShell.Main`), `config/index.ts` (`docs`, `links`), `app/layout.tsx` (forced light, the release banner), `app/global.css` (the banner, the header, the active sidebar row, the docs' amber headings).
- **No `<main>` in a page**: the shell's `AppShell.Main` is every page's `main`.
- **Every Markdown picture is a `/public` path**, imported by the engine's `remark-static-images` and drawn by `DocsImage`: zoomable, a 2x capture at its size in points, with `sizes` for the engine's column (`docsSizes`). A layout change in `components/shell` changes that column: update `STRETCHES` with it.
- **Release notes** are compiled at build time with `marked` (`load-releases.ts`) and join the table of contents through `data-toc-entry`; the hook's runtime fallback loads the compiler only when the build could not reach GitHub.

### Environment

- `GITHUB_TOKEN` (Vercel, build and runtime): `load-releases.ts` fetches the releases at build time, and `/api/github-releases` (the browser fallback) and `/download` use it at runtime; without it GitHub allows 60 requests an hour.
- The Netfox Goodies shop (`/goodies`, its licence and thank-you pages, `/api/goodies/*`): `GOODIES_*` and `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, listed in the headers of `lib/goodies.ts` and `lib/goodies-mail.ts`. Without them every shop route answers 404; a test-mode key keeps the pages out of search results and the sitemap. The shop's pages are built with the settings they find, so a changed setting needs a redeploy.
- **The shop counts its own sales and downloads** (`lib/goodies-events.ts`): GitHub counts no download of a private release's files through its API (every asset read 0 after real downloads, 2026-11-07), so the webhook and `/api/goodies/download` send server-side Web Analytics custom events, `Goodies purchase` and `Goodies download`, each naming its buyer by a 12-hex hash of the session id, never the id. The macOS Studio reads them back through `vercel api /v1/query/web-analytics/events/aggregate`. Only production counts; a preview's events are `environment: preview`.

### Performance

- **Baseline** (production build, Lighthouse mobile, devtools throttling): home perf 96-97, LCP 1.87-1.90 s, 644 KiB; docs 99, 622 KiB; SEO 100.

### Newsletter

The release newsletter is Netfox's Substack (`config.community.newsletter`, `netfoxapp.substack.com`: `netfox.substack.com` is someone else's); nothing on the site collects an address. Ported from lancetta-website#113 with its later fixes: a prompt that opens once after 1200px of scroll, with the Goodies as a promotion above the newsletter (left out on the shop's own pages; `GoodiesCallToAction.module.css` says what moves, once), and once closed stays closed for 12 hours (`NewsletterSignup/NewsletterModal.tsx`, `prompt-open.ts`), its dialog loaded only on open (`PromptDialog.tsx`: five traps in its header, all read in Chrome), a footer band and icon, a Community menu entry, and the corner fox waiting while the prompt is open. `scripts/shot.mjs` stores the prompt as just closed; `--prompt` leaves it as a first visit gets it.

### Motion

`components/Motion`: nothing waits on a script to be seen. Read the headers of `useReveal.ts` and `Motion.module.css` before touching a pose; `Motion.css.test.ts` holds the shape. To fake scripts that never arrive (`scripts/shot.mjs --block`), block the JS only, never the whole chunks folder: the CSS is served from it too, and the page comes back unstyled rather than broken.

### The fox

`components/Mascot`: every behaviour is documented in its headers.
- **To drive it in `shot.mjs --eval`**: click Next by `[aria-label="Next translation"]`, scoped to the fox you mean (corner: `[data-phase][class*="corner"]`, card: `#sponsors [data-phase]`); an unscoped click hits the hero's off-screen copy, and `[class*=next]` can match other classes first.

### Tutorials in the docs

`<Tutorial n={N} />` puts a Netfox Tutorial (the YouTube series, `components/Tutorial/tutorials.ts`) in the docs section that covers it: the poster and a Play pill until clicked, nothing from YouTube before that, a VideoObject in the served HTML. A film is private until its `published` time and an early embed shows "Video unavailable", so each one joins its page on the day it goes out; `Tutorial.test.tsx` fails a page that embeds one sooner. Posters are `public/tutorials/netfox-tutorial-NN.jpg`, 1280x720, through ImageOptim.

## Content Guidelines

- All website content is in **English**
- The app is described as: "A native network monitor for macOS"
- Key selling points: device discovery (Bonjour + ARP + active probing), per-device history timeline, alerts for new devices, native macOS UI, no cloud account required, no telemetry
- Target audience: home network users who want to know who's connected, when, and from where — at a glance
- Download links point to GitHub Releases on the **website** repo (the app repo is private): `https://github.com/gfazioli/netfox-website/releases/latest`

### No infrastructure leaks in user-facing copy

User-facing pages (`content/*.mdx`, the homepage, release notes hosted at `public/release-notes/<version>.html`, FAQ entries, marketing CTAs) **never name the underlying provider, model, or infrastructure**:

- ❌ "Groq", "Llama", "OpenAI", "Anthropic" — say "the AI" or "the AI provider"
- ❌ "Vercel proxy", "Next.js API route", "Cloudflare Worker" — say "Netfox handles the request on your behalf"
- ❌ "Sparkle", "AppKit's NSEvent monitor", framework names — say "the auto-update framework" / "macOS keyboard handling"
- ✅ User-relevant facts ARE allowed: "free", "no account required", "data never leaves your Mac", "macOS 15.6+ required"

Reasoning: end users care about what the feature does for them, not which vendor or library powers it. Naming the stack also paints us into a corner if we ever swap it — would force rewriting every page.

**Exceptions**:
- Developer-facing files (commit messages, this `AGENTS.md`) — name infra freely
- "Under the hood" sections at the bottom of release notes — okay to be specific for power users who want to know, but prefer generic phrasing where it doesn't lose information
- **`SwiftUI` stays in `BuiltForMacSection` and the Welcome feature grid**: there the name is the claim (a real Mac app, not an Electron wrapper). Elsewhere drop it when it only explains an implementation. Reviewers flag it; it has been considered.
